about: Every departure from the server guide that the Brennan's pack makes, each with its reason and its source, so a reader can audit the pack against the guide (house/brennans/guide.txt, menus read 26 September 2026) and the research under house/brennans/research/. The builder (house/build-brennans.mjs) applies the entries in order after parsing and before dash stripping; a replace whose 'from' is not found fails the build. Verdict ids (chef-dishes-b-4, gap-pron-6 and so on) are the ids in research/verified-facts.json; 'pdf-corrections pN' points at research/pdf-corrections.json by page. A still-unverifiable fact is placed nowhere as a fact; a refuted claim appears only as its correction. Prices are never touched here. Targets: house | dish:<name> | wine:<name> | cocktail:<name> | tasting:<name> | term:<term> | scenario:<title> | mixup:<a> vs <b> | mustknow:<title> | <list>:+ to add. Ops: set (default), replace {from,to}, append, add. From the 3 October 2026 edition, an add on dish:+ or cocktail:+ files a whole item the guide prints only as a price line or a must-know, or a house page the research read prints (the 1946 list, the Luxury Roost Bar cocktails, the premium Sazeracs, the eye openers, the coffees and juice, the children's menu, the Bubbles snacks); every such price stands verbatim on guide.txt or on a snapshot under house/brennans/pages/ whose first line names its source.

principles.reason: The guide prints five pairing principles outside the engine's nine. In the guide's own formula (p3) bubbles sit under Fat (butter and fried food want acidity or bubbles), umami under Salt & umami, and smoke is listed under Bridge (a shared flavour: herbs, citrus, smoke, mushroom, butter, toast), so each maps there when the block does not already carry that principle; temp and texture have no home among the nine and are dropped. entries.value: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant on Bourbon Street in July 1946, and it has been at 417 Royal Street since 1956. Owen died in November 1955, before the move; Ella Brennan found the backing and the family opened Royal Street in 1956. The building dates from 1795, was the first bank in Louisiana and later the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; the bank's initials survive in the balcony ironwork. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's widow Maude and sons Pip, Jimmy and Ted kept Royal Street, and Ella's side took Commander's Palace. Brennan's closed in June 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after a restoration of the whole house. Paul Blange, the first chef, created Bananas Foster and Eggs Hussarde; Michael Roussel, Lazone Randolph, Slade Rushing and Ryan Hacker followed him, and Kris Padalino has led the kitchen since June 2025. 2026 is the 80th year.
entries.reason: The history the guide omits: Owen's death in 1955, the 2013 closure and the November 2014 reopening under Ralph Brennan and Terry White, the building of 1795 and Paul Morphy, the family split, the chef lineage

entries.value: Invented here in 1951, when Owen Brennan asked his sister Ella and chef Paul Blange for a banana dessert, and named for his friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission (also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission). entries.value: Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. value.q: What is the classic Sazerac build, and is it ours?
value.a: The Classic Sazerac at Brennan's is Sazerac rye stirred with Peychaud's bitters, served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint (ERB-saint), $13; confirm sugar and lemon peel with the bar. The Sazerac Company's own recipe is a sugar cube, three dashes of Peychaud's, an ounce and a half of Sazerac Rye, a quarter ounce of Herbsaint and a lemon peel, built across two glasses and served neat in a chilled rocks glass; the IBA version is Cognac based with absinthe. Give those as the classic, never as the house build. If a guest asks for it on the rocks, check with the bar before promising it. Two luxury versions: Thompson's Dream with Willett rye, and Origin Story with Cognac and absinthe; the price ladder is $13, $20 and $40.

value.title: The chefs
value.body: Paul Blangé, the chef behind Bananas Foster, led the kitchen until the 1970s. Michael Roussel, who started here in 1956 and trained under Blangé, became executive chef in 1974 and retired in 2005 after 49 years. Lazone Randolph, who began as a dishwasher in 1965, succeeded him in 2005 and gave his name to Chicken Lazone. Slade Rushing ran the kitchen from the 2014 reopening to 2019 and Ryan Hacker from late 2019 to spring 2025. Our executive chef is Kris Padalino, who took over in June 2025 after eight years in this kitchen as pastry chef and executive sous chef; she trained at Le Cordon Bleu in Pasadena and cooked in Los Angeles and Denver before New Orleans.

value.title: The building and the family
value.body: 1795: it was Louisiana's first bank, then the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; look for the bank's initials in the balcony ironwork. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's side kept Royal Street, Ella's side took Commander's Palace; Brennan's of Houston belongs to Ella's side, so a guest who ate at Brennan's in Houston ate at a cousin. The house closed on 28 June 2013 and reopened on 25 November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after seventeen months of restoration.

lines.s45: Our cocktail list is themed Summer Vacations of 1946, the year Brennan's opened, and the Yellowstone is the national park trip. It's Uncle Nearest 1884, a small batch whiskey, with fresh lemon, a honey and turmeric syrup we make here, and Peychaud's Aperitivo, a bittersweet red aperitif under the same New Orleans name as our Sazerac bitters.
